judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The image is the only content of a link (target _blank) to mantissolutions.com, after the visible words "Powered By" in the header of the Mantis "Similar articles to this" widget; its alt "Mantis Logo" is the link's whole name, so the claim holds of the capture: the alt names the logo and does not spell out a destination. For a linked logo, naming the organisation is enough to tell where the link goes (the Mantis site), and "Powered By" beside it gives the role; the extra word "Logo" is a best-practice nit, not a 1.1.1 failure. The live HTML holds the same mantis-ui-widget placeholder that a script fills, and the styled screenshot shows the widget as captured; nothing suggests a difference. The checker applied a stricter rule (the alt must state the destination outright) than 1.1.1 requires.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: Article photo of Lee Palmer, a bald bearded man in a grey hoodie at the open door of number 18; the alt repeats the visible caption, a statement of what Lee said about the post. The claim holds of the capture: the erratic postal service the alt talks about is not something the photo shows. But the alt does name Lee, the person pictured, right after the paragraph that introduces him, so it arguably serves the photo's purpose in a news story (who this is), while saying nothing about the scene. Auditors split on caption-as-alt for portraits like this; I lean towards a pass, but the disagreement is reasonable, so uncertain. The live HTML has the same img and alt, and the styled screenshot matches the crop.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Thumbnail (a person walking on a snowy path, matching its src, Sefton Park in snow) inside a recommendation-card link that has aria-label "'Coldest night' in Liverpool so far with -4C forecast overnight" and also holds the visible headline. The alt "Find more about <headline>" describes the article rather than the picture, so the sentence is true of the capture. But the image is functional: it is part of a link whose purpose the alt states correctly, and the link's aria-label overrides it anyway, so screen readers announce the headline. 1.1.1 asks a functional image's alternative to convey its function, which this one does; describing the snow scene is not required. The widget is script-injected; the live HTML has its placeholder and nothing suggests the capture differs. The checker applied a stricter rule (describe the visual content).

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The card image's srcset is 3_The-birds-in-the-aviary.jpg (fetched: two green parakeets on a perch inside an aviary), but the crop the model saw shows an unrelated game-like street scene: the carousel auto-advances (the screenshot shows the cards at other positions than the snapshot bounds) and the crop caught another slide. Against that crop the claim holds; against the real image, the aviary the alt names is shown. Either way the image is functional, inside a link with aria-label equal to the headline, and "Find more about <headline>" states the link's purpose, so 1.1.1 is met. The wrong crop is a capture difference that bears on this claim, hence collector_error (the sibling cards show the same stricter reading of 1.1.1 as well).

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The header premium button: an SVG showing the word SUBSCRIBE with the liver-bird mark, alt "liverpoolecho", the only content of a link to /subscribe that has aria-label "Subscribe to premium membership". The claim is true of the capture: the alt names the brand and leaves out the "Subscribe" the image conveys. But the link's aria-label names the control and overrides the img alt, so assistive technology announces "Subscribe to premium membership, link", which conveys the image's function (ARIA6). The alt is mismatched and alt="" would be cleaner, but there is no 1.1.1 failure. The header is rendered by script (absent from the live server HTML) but the styled capture shows it, and nothing suggests a difference. The model had the link's name in the context and judged the image alone.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Desktop primary-nav link "Things To Do" (uppercase by CSS) to /whats-on/, the What's On hub. In the capture, besides two hidden MoreCurtain copies, three links carry this text: this one and the mobile-nav "Things To Do" (both /whats-on/) and the mobile-nav submenu "Things to do" (/all-about/things-to-do-liverpool); no heading or label sits near this one, so the sentence holds. But 2.4.4 does not require unique link text (Understanding 2.4.4 only says different text "helps"): this link's purpose, the site's things-to-do section, is clear from its text, and both destinations are things-to-do listings. The other two links are in the mobile nav, inert (out of focus order and the accessibility tree) until opened, where the sublink is nested under "Things To Do" (H81). The live HTML matches. The checker applied a stricter rule (unique text).

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Article photo of Wylva Road: a terraced street of brick houses under a grey sky, wheelie bins with a "Local residents use only" sign, parked cars. The photo is informative (it shows the street the story is about) and nothing else describes it; an alternative that conveys none of its content does not serve the equivalent purpose, so 1.1.1 fails, and the claim (the alt describes something the image does not show) names that failure. The live HTML has the same img and alt; the styled screenshot matches the crop.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The logo at the top of the consent dialog ("Take control of your privacy"): the red ECHO wordmark with the liver bird, alt "Publisher Logo". The claim's sentence is false of the capture: the image is a publisher logo, so the alt does not describe something absent. But the alt is generic placeholder text that leaves out the one thing the logo conveys, the publication's name (ECHO / Liverpool Echo), which appears nowhere else in the dialog's text; that fails 1.1.1 (in the spirit of F30). Read in good faith, as the rubric's own example puts it, an alternative said to describe what the image does not show when it leaves out what the image conveys names this defect. The dialog is script-injected; the styled screenshot shows it as captured and nothing suggests a difference.
